intro: This guide walks a Sunday school class, homeschool group or family through “The Practice of the Presence of God (For Children)” in twelve weeks, one chapter a week. It works for a small family around the table or a class of up to twenty, and is best for ages 6–12; the youngest will enjoy the action games, and older children can do more of the writing.

Each session takes about 30 minutes. Welcome everyone and say the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter aloud (5–7 minutes). Talk together using the chapter’s three questions (5–10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or your own (2 minutes).

To prepare, read the chapter yourself beforehand and have paper, pencils and crayons ready; a few weeks need nothing at all. The book is gentle throughout, but the last two chapters talk about illness, danger and Brother Lawrence’s death in old age, so read them calmly, answer questions simply and truthfully, and keep coming back to the book’s one big idea: God is with us all through the day, in every ordinary job and every hard moment.

weeks.summary: We meet Lawrence as a young footman, a servant who waited on an important treasurer, Monsieur Fieubert. He was big and clumsy and called himself “a great awkward fellow who broke everything,” yet God was not looking at his clumsy hands but at his heart. The big idea: God doesn’t love us because we are clever or careful; he looks at the heart and can use anyone.

memory_verse.text: The LORD, you have searched me, and you know me.

activity.title: What God Sees
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half.
On the front, draw yourself doing something you find tricky, like spilling a drink or dropping a ball.
Inside, draw a big heart and write “God looks at my heart.”
Colour the heart in and take your card home as a reminder that God loves you just as you are.

weeks.summary: At eighteen, in winter, Lawrence looks at a bare tree and thinks about how its leaves, flowers and fruit will come back in spring. He suddenly sees how strong God is and how faithfully he looks after everything he has made, and that thought filled him with a love for God that lasted the rest of his life. The big idea: the things God made around us can show us how great and kind he is.

memory_verse.text: The LORD, how many are your works! In wisdom have you made them all. The earth is full of your riches.

activity.title: Bare Tree, Full Tree
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half so you have two sides.
On the left side, draw a bare winter tree with brown branches and no leaves.
On the right side, draw the same tree in spring and summer, with green leaves, flowers and fruit.
Write “God looks after what he made” across the bottom.
Share your trees with a neighbour and say one other thing God made that you will look out for this week.

weeks.summary: Lawrence joins a monastery and becomes “Brother” Lawrence, expecting to be told off for his clumsiness and ready to give up every pleasure for God, even if it made him miserable. Instead God “disappointed” him in the best way: he found nothing but happiness there. The big idea: God is not a grumpy king; being close to him is the happiest place there is.

memory_verse.text: You will show me the path of life. In your presence is fullness of joy. In your right hand there are pleasures forevermore.

activity.title: Grumpy King or Kind Father?
steps: Explain the game: if a sentence is true about God, stand up tall with a big smile; if it is not true, crouch down with a grumpy face.
Call out sentences such as “God loves to give us joy,” “God only wants us to be sad,” “God is kind,” “God gets cross every time we make a mistake,” “God is happy when we come close to him.”
After each one, say briefly why it is or isn’t true.
Finish by everyone standing tall, smiling, and saying the memory verse together.

weeks.summary: Brother Lawrence reads lots of books about coming close to God, but they all say different things and only muddle him. So he keeps it simple: he gives himself to God and lives as if there were only God and him, thinking of God as often as he can. It was not easy; his mind wandered and for years he worried, but he kept trusting until a deep, quiet peace filled his heart. The big idea: loving God doesn’t need clever rules; we can simply remember he is with us and tell him we love him.

memory_verse.text: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.

activity.title: A Quiet Minute with God
steps: Sit comfortably, close your eyes or look down at your hands, and keep very still.
For one minute, while the leader keeps time, tell God silently in your heart, “God, you are here, and I love you.”
If your mind wanders off, don’t worry: just come back and say it again, like Brother Lawrence did.
When the minute is up, talk together about how it felt and whether it was hard to stay still.
Choose one quiet moment this week, such as bedtime, to try it again at home.

weeks.summary: The monastery makes clumsy Brother Lawrence the cook, a job he naturally disliked. His secret was to plan his work, then ask God to stay close to him, help him, and take all his work as a gift; he kept talking to God quietly as he worked, and the job became easy. He did it for fifteen years. The big idea: any job, even one we don’t like, can become a gift of love to God when we ask his help and do it for him.

memory_verse.text: Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men.

activity.title: Chore Prayers
steps: Together, name some jobs children don’t always like, such as tidying a bedroom, making the bed or putting shoes away.
Make up a short “chore prayer” for each one, like Brother Lawrence’s, for example “God, you are here with me; help me do this for you.”
Everyone mimes doing one of the jobs while saying the chore prayer quietly.
Each child chooses one chore and one chore prayer to use at home this week.

weeks.summary: Brother Lawrence said he was glad to pick up even a single straw from the ground for the love of God. He taught that God doesn’t look at how big a job is but at how much love it is done with, so stirring a pot or sweeping a floor can be done for God. The big idea: small, everyday things done out of love for God are precious to him, and children can do them today.

memory_verse.text: Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.

activity.title: Straws on the Floor
activity.materials: A few sheets of scrap paper, scrunched into small balls
steps: Before the game, scatter the scrunched paper “straws” around the room.
On “Go,” children walk (not run) and pick up one piece at a time.
Each time someone picks one up, they say “For you, God!”
When the floor is tidy, sit down and each name one small job you could do for God at home or school this week.

weeks.summary: Dinner time in the monastery kitchen is noisy, with pots and pans clattering and several people calling for different things at once, yet Brother Lawrence stays calm, never rushing and never lazy. He prayed in his heart all the time and said, put simply, that in the noise and clatter of his kitchen he had God as peacefully as if he were on his knees. The big idea: prayer isn’t only for quiet, special times; we can stay close to God in the busy, noisy parts of our day.

activity.title: Noisy Kitchen, Quiet Heart
steps: Pretend the room is a busy monastery kitchen: everyone mimes stirring pretend pots and clattering pretend pans, making kitchen noises.
When the leader calls “Quiet heart!”, everyone freezes and whispers, “God, you are here with me.”
On “Kitchen!”, start the noisy pretend work again; repeat three or four times.
Talk together about the busiest, noisiest moment in your own day, and agree to whisper a prayer then this week.

weeks.summary: In letters to his friends, Brother Lawrence explains that talking with God is simpler than we think: we don’t need to shout, because God is very near, and we can make our hearts into a little prayer room. His prayers were often short, like “My God, here I am, all yours,” and he said it would be rude to leave a visiting friend sitting alone, so we shouldn’t leave God alone either. The big idea: practising the presence of God means remembering he is here and talking with him like a friend.

memory_verse.text: The LORD is near to all those who call on him, to all who call on him in truth.

activity.title: My Heart Prayer Room
steps: Draw a big heart and turn it into a little room, with a door, a window and something cosy inside.
Draw yourself in the room, and show that God is there with you, perhaps with light or warm colours.
On the door, write a short prayer of your own, like “God, here I am, all yours.”
Take it home and use your door prayer whenever you remember God this week.

weeks.summary: Brother Lawrence is sent to Burgundy to buy the community’s wine, a business job he felt he was no good at, and his lame leg meant that on the boat he could only get about by rolling himself over the barrels. Instead of worrying, he told God it was God’s business and trusted him with it, and it went very well, as an earlier trip to Auvergne had too. The big idea: when a job feels too hard for us, we can give our worries to God and trust him to help.

memory_verse.text: Casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.

activity.title: A Boat Full of Worries
steps: Draw a boat on the water with several round barrels on its deck.
Inside each barrel, draw or write something that feels hard or worrying for you; this picture is just for you and God.
Across the side of the boat write “God’s business” and draw a smiling sun above it.
Fold your picture and hold it while the leader prays, giving all the worries to God.

weeks.summary: Brother Lawrence wasn’t perfect: sometimes he forgot God for a long time or did things he knew were wrong. When he did, he didn’t sulk, give up or make excuses; he simply told God, asked for help, then stopped worrying and went back to loving God, trusting that his sins were forgiven because of Jesus. By getting up again after every fall, little by little, he learned to think about God all the time. Keep this week’s talk general and never ask children to name their own wrong things aloud. The big idea: when we get it wrong, we can tell God, trust Jesus to forgive us, and start again.

memory_verse.text: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

activity.title: Wobble and Start Again
steps: Everyone stands and tries to balance on one foot while the leader counts slowly.
When you wobble or put your foot down, say “Start again!” and try once more, just as Brother Lawrence got up after every fall.
Sit down and, on paper, draw a bright sunrise with the words “Jesus forgives. I can start again.”
Keep the picture somewhere private at home to remember on a day when you get it wrong.

weeks.summary: Older now, Brother Lawrence writes letters to friends in hard times. He tells one that a young soldier in danger can lift up his heart to God for a moment even while marching, and that short prayers make him braver; he tells a friend who is very ill that God is often nearer in sickness than in health, and prays for strength and patience to bear the pain, trusting God as a loving Father. Handle this gently: some children may know someone who is ill, so let them share only if they want to and keep the focus on God being close. The big idea: God stays near when we are sick, sad or scared, and even “Help me, God” is a prayer he hears.

memory_verse.text: Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.

activity.title: A Get-Well Prayer Card
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half to make a card.
On the front, draw something cheerful, such as flowers, a rainbow or a sunny window.
Inside, write a very short prayer, like Brother Lawrence’s, such as “God is near you. Help them, God.”
Give the card to someone who is ill or having a hard time, or keep it to pray for them yourself.

weeks.summary: Brother Lawrence grows old, almost eighty, and has walked with God for more than forty years since he saw the bare tree. Often ill, he asked not for the pain to go but for strength to bear it, and said he was always happy because God was with him; soon after his last letters he died and went home to be with God. His letters kept giving the same invitation: think of God often, talk with him, trust him, “Let us begin.” Speak of his death simply and peacefully, as the chapter does, as going home to the God he loved. The big idea: Brother Lawrence’s invitation is for children too; anyone can begin today.

memory_verse.text: In my Father’s house are many mansions. If it weren’t so, I would have told you. I am going to prepare a place for you.

activity.title: My Day with God
steps: Draw a winding path across your paper, from waking up at one end to bedtime at the other.
Along the path, draw five or six stops from your ordinary day, such as breakfast, getting dressed, school, a chore and playtime.
At each stop, write or draw a tiny prayer or a way you could notice God there.
Put a star at the stop where you will “begin” this week, and share it with the group if you would like to.
